prompt: Which of these is a direct dependency of the linkbox service?

choices.text: werkzeug
choices.why: Flask needs it; `app.py` never names it, so it is transitive although `requirements.txt` pins it.

choices.text: markupsafe
choices.why: Jinja and Werkzeug bring it in.

choices.text: gunicorn
choices.why: Right. The Dockerfile starts it by name, so the service depends on it directly.

choices.text: packaging
choices.why: gunicorn and pytest pull it in, and no file names it.

prompt: How many packages did the two requirements files of lesson 1 put in the environment, transitive ones included?
pytest is not in linkbox's image. Why does the lesson audit `requirements-dev.txt` anyway?

choices.text: pip-audit refuses to audit one file without the other
choices.why: It audits whatever `-r` files it is given, one or several.

choices.text: It runs where the credentials are
choices.why: Right: on the CI machine, beside the pipeline's credentials. A flaw in a test tool is a flaw on the build machine.

choices.text: The image copies the whole repository, tests included
choices.why: The image installs only `requirements.txt`; pytest is never installed in it.

choices.text: Development dependencies have more advisories than others
choices.why: There is no such rule; here one dev package had one flaw.

prompt: pip-audit printed 29 rows for lesson 1's `requirements.txt`. Why does that not mean 29 flaws?

choices.text: pip-audit audits each package twice, once per file
choices.why: It was given one file here, and the rows still doubled.

choices.text: Some rows are for versions that are not installed
choices.why: Every row names the installed version.

choices.text: Most flaws arrive as two records, GHSA and PYSEC
choices.why: Right. PyPI serves both and pip-audit prints a row each. Counting distinct CVE ids gives fifteen.

choices.text: Withdrawn advisories are still listed
choices.why: Nothing in the run was withdrawn; the duplicates are aliases.

prompt: How many distinct CVE ids did the audit of lesson 1's `requirements.txt` come down to?
Match each kind of identifier to what it is.

pairs.right: one id per flaw, across every language and product
GitHub's reviewed advisory for a package ecosystem
the Python Packaging Authority's advisory for a PyPI package
a shared format, and a service that gathers the others

right_distractors: a score from 0 to 10 for how bad the flaw is

prompt: `pip-audit` reports no known vulnerabilities for a project. What does that result assert?

choices.text: The dependencies contain no exploitable flaw
choices.why: A flaw nobody has disclosed passes every audit.

choices.text: No advisory it knows of matched these versions
choices.why: Right. SCA finds only what has been disclosed, in the database it asked, on that day.

choices.text: Every package has been reviewed by its maintainers
choices.why: Advisories say nothing about reviews of what is clean.

choices.text: The project's own code is free of injection flaws
choices.why: pip-audit never reads the project's code; that is lesson 3's job.

prompt: Why is the Flask advisory CVE-2026-27205 not reachable in linkbox?

choices.text: linkbox sets `Cache-Control: private` on every page
choices.why: linkbox sets no `Cache-Control` at all; the headers of lesson 4 are three others.

choices.text: `app.py` never touches the session
choices.why: Right. The advisory needs session keys read, and linkbox has no session.

choices.text: gunicorn strips the `Vary` header
choices.why: gunicorn passes headers through; the condition fails much earlier.

choices.text: Flask 3.0.0 predates the flaw
choices.why: The audit says 3.0.0 is affected and 3.1.3 fixes it.

prompt: Which change to linkbox would make its three Jinja template flaws (CVE-2024-56201, CVE-2024-56326, CVE-2025-27516) reachable?

choices.text: Moving the service to a Windows server
choices.why: Windows matters to Werkzeug's `safe_join` flaws, not to these.

choices.text: Putting a caching proxy in front of it
choices.why: A cache is a condition of the Flask flaw.

choices.text: Letting users save page templates that Jinja renders
choices.why: Right. All three need an attacker able to write a template.

choices.text: Adding a second search box to the page
choices.why: A value in a template is escaped data; these flaws need control of the template itself.

prompt: Twelve of linkbox's fifteen flaws are not reachable today. What does the lesson use that judgement for?

choices.text: To skip those twelve upgrades
choices.why: Each has a cheap fix, and a later commit can make any of them reachable.

choices.text: To order the work, and judge findings with no fix
choices.why: Right. Reachability decides what comes first and what may wait when nothing can be upgraded.

choices.text: To mark them IGNORE in the rules the scanner reads
choices.why: pip-audit has no such file here, and the reasoning would be lost.

choices.text: To lower their CVSS scores
choices.why: CVSS base scores are the sources' to set; nothing here changes them.

prompt: Match each signal to the question it answers.

pairs.right: how bad would it be if exploited
how likely is exploitation in the next 30 days
has it been exploited in the wild

right_distractors: does this service reach the vulnerable code

prompt: Trivy's report scores CVE-2024-1135 at 8.2 from GitHub and 7.5 from Red Hat. Why two numbers?

choices.text: One uses CVSS 3.1 and the other 2.0
choices.why: Both vectors are version 3; they differ in one letter.

choices.text: They judged the confidentiality impact differently
choices.why: Right: `C:L` against `C:N`, from the same description.

choices.text: Red Hat lowers its scores for its own paying customers
choices.why: Each source scores the flaw as it reads it; nothing here is per customer.

choices.text: One includes EPSS and the other does not
choices.why: EPSS is a separate probability and never enters a CVSS score.

prompt: How many of linkbox's fifteen CVEs were in CISA's KEV catalogue on the day of the recording?
Two findings, time for one fix today. A: CVSS 9.8, not on KEV, code not reachable. B: CVSS 6.5, on KEV, code reachable. Both have a fixed version. Which first, by the lesson's order?

choices.text: A, because its score is higher
choices.why: The score says how bad if exploited; B is being exploited, and you reach it.

choices.text: Neither, until EPSS is checked
choices.why: KEV is already stronger evidence than any probability.

choices.text: A, because unreachable code can become reachable
choices.why: True of both; it does not change which is urgent today.

choices.text: B
choices.why: Right. On KEV comes first whatever its score, and this one is on a path the service runs.

prompt: Trivy's summary for `requirements-dev.txt` shows `-` under Vulnerabilities. What does that mean?

choices.text: The file was not scanned at all
choices.why: Right. Trivy recognises `requirements.txt` by name, and this file is not that name.

choices.text: The file was scanned and found clean
choices.why: Clean is `0`; the legend under the table says so.

choices.text: Trivy's database has no Python advisories
choices.why: It found fifteen in `requirements.txt` a moment earlier.

choices.text: pytest has no advisory in Trivy's database
choices.why: Trivy never looked pytest up; pip-audit found its advisory.

prompt: Given a file with the single line `flask==3.0.0`, pip-audit audited seven packages and Trivy one. Why?

choices.text: pip-audit counts duplicate advisories as packages
choices.why: The seven are package names with versions, not advisories.

choices.text: Trivy skips packages without advisories
choices.why: It listed Flask, which has one, and nothing else exists in its view of the file.

choices.text: pip-audit resolves what would be installed; Trivy reads the lines
choices.why: Right. One audits the resolution today, the other what the file says.

choices.text: Trivy needs a lock file to see Flask's dependencies
choices.why: A lock file would name them, and then Trivy would read them; it does not resolve either way.

prompt: A project's `requirements.txt` pins only its direct dependencies. pip-audit passes on Monday and fails on Thursday; nobody committed in between. What is the most likely explanation from this lesson?

choices.text: pip-audit's cache expired
choices.why: A cache changes speed, not which packages are audited.

choices.text: A transitive package moved, or an advisory appeared
choices.why: Right. Unpinned packages move, and the database grows; a lock file removes the first cause.

choices.text: Trivy's database was updated
choices.why: pip-audit asks PyPI, not Trivy's database.

choices.text: The direct pins were rewritten by pip during install
choices.why: pip never edits a requirements file.

prompt: Put the steps of the minimal move in order.
items: set each flagged package to its highest fixed version
read what the new versions require

prompt: The pip-audit option in `ci/sca.sh` that makes the audit fail when a dependency could not be collected is ___
After the move, `pip-audit -r requirements.txt` was clean, and the first push still broke the build in `sca`. Why?

choices.text: The CI resolved newer versions, and they were vulnerable
choices.why: Every version in `requirements.txt` is pinned; the CI installed the same ones.

choices.text: pytest 8.4.2, in the second file, had an advisory
choices.why: Right. The stage audits `requirements-dev.txt` too, and that file had never been audited.

choices.text: `--strict` failed on a package it could not find on PyPI
choices.why: The log shows a vulnerability row, not a collection failure.

choices.text: The image still had Flask 3.0.0 in it
choices.why: `sca` reads the requirements files and runs before the build.

prompt: Which of these changes belong to linkbox's minimal move? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: itsdangerous from 2.1.2 to 2.2.0
choices.why: Right: Flask 3.1.3 asks for 2.2.0 or later, as its metadata says.

choices.text: click to its newest release
choices.why: click had no advisory and the new Flask accepts 8.1.7, so it stays.

choices.text: blinker from 1.7.0 to 1.9.0
choices.why: Right: Flask 3.1.3 asks for 1.9.0 or later.

choices.text: markupsafe to 3.x
choices.why: It had no advisory and nothing required more than 2.1.3.

prompt: A week from now, a push that only edits the README fails in `sca`. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The README is audited as a requirements file
choices.why: pip-audit reads only the files given with `-r`.

choices.text: An advisory was published for a version already pinned
choices.why: Right. The audit asks what is known today, and what is known grows.

choices.text: The pins drifted because they lack hashes
choices.why: A pinned version installs that version; hashes are about the file's bytes, lesson 15.

choices.text: pip-audit fails every run after seven days without a dependency change
choices.why: No such rule exists; the stage fails on findings.

prompt: A teammate wants to leave Werkzeug at 3.0.1 because "the `safe_join` flaws are Windows-only and we run Linux". A fixed version exists. What does the lesson answer?

choices.text: Agree: unreachable findings need no action
choices.why: They need a decision, and with a cheap fix the decision is to move.

choices.text: Agree, and set the rule to IGNORE
choices.why: There is no rule file in this stage, and IGNORE would hide the reachable one too.

choices.text: Upgrade: one Werkzeug flaw is reachable, and the fix costs a test run
choices.why: Right. CVE-2024-49767 is on the form path, and the move is six lines and green tests.

choices.text: Wait for EPSS to rise above a threshold
choices.why: EPSS was not even reachable here, and the fix is already available.
